4. Regression re-specification
Let us transform acrePrice and acres variables with the log transformation and estimate the regression again. The old regression is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{acrePrice} &= \alpha + \beta_{1}(\operatorname{crpPct}) + \beta_{2}(\operatorname{acres})\ + \\
&\quad \beta_{3}(\operatorname{region}_{\operatorname{West\ Central}}) + \beta_{4}(\operatorname{region}_{\operatorname{Central}}) + \beta_{5}(\operatorname{region}_{\operatorname{South\ West}})\ + \\
&\quad \beta_{6}(\operatorname{region}_{\operatorname{South\ Central}}) + \beta_{7}(\operatorname{region}_{\operatorname{South\ East}}) + \beta_{8}(\operatorname{tillable})\ + \\
&\quad \beta_{9}(\operatorname{productivity}) + \epsilon
\end{aligned}
\]

Write down the new regression equation with the transformations.


\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{log(acrePrice)} &= \alpha + \beta_{1}(\operatorname{crpPct}) + \beta_{2}(\operatorname{\log(acres)})\ + \\
&\quad \beta_{3}(\operatorname{region}_{\operatorname{West\ Central}}) + \beta_{4}(\operatorname{region}_{\operatorname{Central}}) + \beta_{5}(\operatorname{region}_{\operatorname{South\ West}})\ + \\
&\quad \beta_{6}(\operatorname{region}_{\operatorname{South\ Central}}) + \beta_{7}(\operatorname{region}_{\operatorname{South\ East}}) + \beta_{8}(\operatorname{tillable})\ + \\
&\quad \beta_{9}(\operatorname{productivity}) + \epsilon
\end{aligned}
\]

1. Problem setting
We would like to evaluate the causal effect of the BIMAS production intensification program on the rice output among rice-producing farmers in India.

The outcome variable is:

goutput - gross output of rice in kg per year produced on the farm.

Key variable of interest is:

bimas variable of interest is an intensification program. Each farmer either participates in it (yes), partially participate (mixed), or does not participate (no).

Other control variables are:

size the total area cultivated with rice, measured in hectares;
urea urea application in kilogram
phosphate phosphate application in kilogram
hiredlabor hired labor in hours
famlabor family labor in hours

title: Week 07. Multiple Linear Regression. Practice.
text:
2. Regression model
The production function is used to estimate the relationship. We consider two main production functions (see Feng and Horrace 2012):


Linear production function, when output is a linear combination of all inputs. (Write it down)



\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{goutput} &= \alpha + \beta_{1}(\operatorname{size}) + \beta_{2}(\operatorname{bimas}_{\operatorname{yes}})\ + \\
&\quad \beta_{3}(\operatorname{bimas}_{\operatorname{mixed}}) + \beta_{4}(\operatorname{famlabor}) + \beta_{5}(\operatorname{hiredlabor})\ + \\
&\quad \beta_{6}(\operatorname{urea}) + \beta_{7}(\operatorname{phosphate}) + \epsilon
\end{aligned}
\]



Cobb-Douglas production function, when the log of output is a linear combination of logged inputs. (Write it down)



\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{log(goutput)} &= \alpha + \beta_{1}(\operatorname{\log(size)}) + \beta_{2}(\operatorname{bimas}_{\operatorname{yes}})\ + \\
&\quad \beta_{3}(\operatorname{bimas}_{\operatorname{mixed}}) + \beta_{4}(\operatorname{\log(famlabor)}) + \beta_{5}(\operatorname{\log(hiredlabor)})\ + \\
&\quad \beta_{6}(\operatorname{\log(urea)}) + \beta_{7}(\operatorname{\log(phosphate)}) + \epsilon
\end{aligned}
\]

text:
Hypothesis testing

What?

Hypothesis Test: A statistical test of the null hypothesis against an alternative hypothesis (Wooldridge 2020).



Why?

We never know the true parameters of the population.
We must infer about the population from samples.
HT establishes certainty behind our inference (probability or an error).



How?

Following Neyman-Pearson’s (Neyman and Pearson 1933) approach to hypothesis testing.

title: Week 04. Cause and Effect in the RCT. Hypothesis testing. T-tests. Exmples. Central Limit Theorem.
text:
Neyman-Pearson’s approach

Assumes that an infinite number of repeated samples can be drawn from the same population.
Aims to minimize the risk of making false conclusions about the relationship.
Controls the probability of error when stating, “we reject the null hypothesis.”

title: Week 04. Cause and Effect in the RCT. Hypothesis testing. T-tests. Exmples. Central Limit Theorem.
text:
Hypothesis Testing: Steps



\(H_0\): Null/Zero Hypothesis;

\(H_0 : \mu = 0\)

\(H_1\): Alternative Hypothesis;

\(H_1 : \mu \ne 0\)

Estimate parameters:

\(\hat \mu = \widehat{\text{mean}}\) , and
\(s = \widehat{\text{SD}}\)

Compute the test statistics;

usually \(t\) statistics




Conclude:

to reject \(H_0 = \text{accept}\, H_1\), or
fail to reject \(H_0 = \text{accept}\, H_0\)

Calculate probabilities of making an error.

probability value (aka “p-value”)

If the paper finds a difference in nutrition statuses between the control and treatment groups, does it mean that education has a causal effect on nutrition?

text:
Checks and balances
To identify that factors (age, education, …) are NOT DIFFERENT between two groups, we need to:

Perform statistical hypothesis testing.
Formulate the hypotheses:

\(H_0\): Factor A in the treatment group is equal to that in the control group.
\(H_1\): Factor A in the treatment group is NOT equal to that in the control group.

Conclude:

text:
Good controls in the RCT
The control group is a perfect counterfactual when three conditions are met:

has the same characteristics, on average, as the treatment group;
remains unaffected by the treatment; and
reacts to the treatment in the same way as the treatment group;



When these three conditions are met, the treatment causes the effect ceteris paribus (Gertler et al. 2016).




the average characteristics of the treatment group and the comparison group must be identical in the absence of the program.2 Although individual units in the treatment group don’t need to have “perfect clones” in the comparison group, on average the characteristics of treatment and comparison groups should be the same.
treatment should not affect the comparison group either directly or indirectly.
the outcomes of units in the control group should change the same way as outcomes in the treatment group if both groups were given the program (or not).

t-tests (1)
Is a statistical test use to conclude about the population based on a sample.

One sample t-test: Compares a population parameter \(\mu\) to an arbitrary number?
Two sample t-test: Compares difference between two parameters \(\mu_1\) and \(\mu_2\) in the population?

Its purpose is to infer:

whether or not the population parameter \(\mu\) (mean, or else)
is different from an arbitrary number (usually zero: \(\mu_{0} = 0\))
based on our sample estimates of

the parameter (\(\widehat{\text{mean}}\)), its variance (\(s\)), and the sample size \(n\).

Significance level: \(\alpha = 0.05\)

\]
where \(se = s / \sqrt{n}\) is the standard error of the estimate;


Step 4: Conclude

Reject \(H_0\) if:

\(|t| > 2\) the “rule of thumb”

The same applies if we say that the estimate is two times larger than the mean.

Statistical hypothesis: basics (1)
As we rely on a samples, we call any measure (mean, median, variance) computed based on such samples as:

the estimates of {\(\text{mean}\), \(\text{median}\), \(\text{variance}\)}. We denote estimates with a “hat” “\(\widehat{\; \; \; \;}"\), for example: {\(\widehat{\text{mean}}\), \(\widehat{\text{median}}\), \(\widehat{\text{variance}}\)}

Statistical hypothesis: basics (2)
To infer that the true {\(\text{mean}\), \(\text{median}\), \(\text{variance}\)} in the population is not different from the estimate of {\(\widehat{\text{mean}}\), \(\widehat{\text{median}}\), \(\widehat{\text{variance}}\)}, we:

formulate two statistical hypothesis:

H0 (the null hypothesis):

“The estimate of {…} is equal to ZERO in the population”.

H1 (the alternative hypothesis):

“The estimate of {…} is NOT equal to zero in the population”.

We accept H0 (fail to reject H0)

because available data is insufficient to reject it;
without implying that H0 is the right hypothesis (Type II error);

title: Week 7 · Multiple linear regression. Practice
text:
What the deck covers

Causal interpretation of the MLR: multiple regression controls only for the factors included in the model; external ceteris paribus is assumed; the regression assumptions restated.
Example 1, a hedonic land prices model: problem setting, regression model formulation, exploratory analysis (summary statistics, regional differences, distributions, scatter plots), estimating the regression, interpreting the results, checking linearity, re-specifying the model and re-checking, and comparing the two models.
Example 2, a production function: problem setting, the regression model and ex-ante hypotheses about the coefficients, exploratory analysis including the effect of the BIMAS programme, estimating the regression and interpreting it coefficient by coefficient, checking linearity, moving to a log specification, interpreting the log model, and conclusions.
Example 3, returns to fertiliser in Kenya: objective and results of the field experiment, whether ceteris paribus is ensured in the RCT, the authors’ regression solution, and checks and balances.
Regression in Excel: a pointer for those who do not use R.

title: Week 5 · Central Limit Theorem. t-distribution. Confidence intervals
text:
What the deck covers

t-test with conditional cash transfers, the example carried over from Week 4.
Normally distributed population and confidence intervals: the population distribution, the 95% interval for the mean, and 90%, 95% and 99% intervals; the population can have any distribution.
The Central Limit Theorem, the standard error, a summary and the CLT in practice.
The confidence interval and the t-distribution: how to find a CI, the t-distribution and how it differs from the normal, from the population to a sample, the t-distribution in use on the travel-time example, interpreting and calculating a confidence interval, and more on the t-distribution and the t-test.

t-scores: critical values of the t-distribution for 1 to 150 degrees of freedom.
Homework on two published field experiments and the key concepts checklist.

title: Week 3 · Bi-variate data. Correlation and causation
text:
What the deck covers

Bi-variate data, introduced with the Palmer penguins, and building a scatter plot step by step.
The scatter plot: what makes a scatter plot self-explaining (title and sources, axis labels and units, points, legends, a temporal dimension), shown with the height and weight of children under three from a nutrition study in Uganda.
Trend lines and examples of describing scatter plots; homework with further examples and drawing a linear trend line.
The correlation coefficient: methodology, interpretation, examples, the non-linearity pitfall and other pitfalls, the correlation matrix, homework and spurious correlations.
Correlation and causation: do we live longer because of a low birth rate? What it takes to establish a causal relationship; insights on the HIV pandemic from Gapminder.
Example: rice yields and fertiliser application: exploratory, univariate and descriptive analysis, the scatter plot, linearity and the linear transformation, correlation exam questions and the causality conclusion.
Cause, effect, potential outcome and ceteris paribus: cause and effect in rice yields, factual and counterfactual outcomes, treatment; randomised control trials, regression and innovation as three routes to ceteris paribus; an RCT example based on a nutrition education trial; potential exam questions.

Each week page brings together the interactive deck, the PDFs of both cohorts, the slide sources and the data behind them.

    Prerequisites
    What to refresh before weeks 1 to 3, with pre-recorded lectures and Khan Academy units, and the additional reading list.
  

  
    Week 1
    Introduction. Descriptive statistics

    Week 2
    Distribution, variance and its applications
    Density and cumulative distributions, the Lorenz curve, variance and standard deviation, quantiles, z-scores and the WHO stunting standards.
  

  
    Week 3
    Bi-variate data. Correlation and causation
    Scatter plots, trend lines, the correlation coefficient and its pitfalls, and the step from correlation to cause, effect and ceteris paribus.
  

  
    Week 4
    Cause and effect in the RCT. Hypothesis testing. t-tests
    Null and alternative hypotheses, the two error types, p-values, and t-tests applied to deworming and conditional cash transfer experiments.
  

  
    Week 5
    Central Limit Theorem. t-distribution. Confidence intervals
    From the population distribution to the sampling distribution of the mean, standard errors, confidence intervals and one- and two-sample t-tests.
  

  
    Week 6
    Simple and multiple regression. Bias. Linearity
    The regression line and OLS, coefficient interpretation and inference, multiple regression, bias versus efficiency, the six assumptions and linearity.
  

  
    Week 7
    Multiple linear regression. Practice
    Three worked examples end to end: hedonic land prices, a rice production function, and returns to fertiliser in a field experiment.

title: Datasets
text:
Provenance

Nutrition surveys (Congo, Brazil, Burkina Faso)
Individual food consumption surveys shared through the FAO/WHO GIFT platform (Global Individual Food consumption data Tool). Prepared by congo-consumption.R, brazil-food-consumption.R and burkin-faso-consumption.R: the consumption file is joined to the subject file and summed to daily intake per subject.
The contributors ask to be acknowledged whenever the data or its derivatives are presented:

Burkina Faso (BFA-00001): Institut de Recherche pour le Développement (IRD); Institut de Recherche en Sciences de la Santé (IRSS); HarvestPlus, International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI), 2016, “The 2010 Food consumption and iron status survey in two provinces of rural Burkina Faso”, doi:10.7910/DVN/5CXCLX.
Democratic Republic of the Congo (COD-00091): University of Colorado School of Medicine, Anschutz Medical Campus and their collaborators in Kinshasa; Sud-Ubangi, Democratic Republic of the Congo; 2014/2016; Women First Dietary Recall Data.







WarningA known quirk of the Congo file



congo-consumption.R reads the Congo consumption file but joins it to the Burkina Faso subject file (line 14 of the script). The country and region columns of congo-nutrition.rds therefore read “Burkina Faso” and its provinces, and the subject attributes (sex, age, weight, height) come from that survey too, while the nutrient columns are from the Congo survey. The slides use only the nutrient columns.




World income distribution
Lakner and Milanovic’s global income distribution, as made available to Our World in Data and published on Max Roser’s website. The data up to 2008 accompany Lakner and Milanovic (2015), Global Income Distribution: From the Fall of the Berlin Wall to the Great Recession, World Bank. The JSON series were saved from the website’s console and parsed by income-distribution.R; the six yearly folders of raw series are in data-raw/income-distribution/.


WHO child growth standards
The length/height-for-age z-score expanded tables for boys and girls from the WHO Child Growth Standards, stacked by who.R.


UN World Population Prospects
Population on 1 January by single age and sex, medium variant, from the UN World Population Prospects 2022, filtered to 1960, 1990 and 2020 by un-population.R. The raw download was too large to keep.


The Datasaurus Dozen
From Matejka and Fitzmaurice (2017), Same Stats, Different Graphs (Autodesk Research), via Alberto Cairo’s Download the Datasaurus.


CFC-11 at Mauna Loa
Monthly mean CFC-11 (F11) mixing ratios by station from the NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory’s HATS programme, gml.noaa.gov.


Not in the repository
Two files the decks read are deliberately excluded by the .gitignore:

materials/data/poverty-population.csv, a country-level extract of extreme poverty rates and population used for the weighted-mean example in Week 1, Part 2. The slide credits Our World in Data and the World Bank’s Poverty and Inequality Platform.
data-raw/uganda-poject/Uganda_B_E_agri and nutrition 04.06.2018.sav, the baseline and endline survey of the Uganda nutrition project used for the scatter-plot section of Week 3 (Jordan et al., 2022, Foods 11(3):344, doi:10.3390/foods11030344). uganda-poject.R explores its variable dictionary.

Two further scripts in data-raw/ are not used by any deck: read-geojson.R (parses SO_geojson_2020_A.json) and summarystata.R (helper for cleaning skimr summaries). title: Week 2 · Distribution, variance and its applications
text:
What the deck covers

Distribution: symmetric and non-symmetric distributions, extreme and influential observations; from a density to a cumulative distribution; the cumulative distribution of income; applications to income inequality and the Lorenz curve, with homework examples.
Variance: population versus sample variance, the standard deviation, and why distributions with the same standard deviation can look very different.
Quantiles: quartiles and deciles for normal and non-normal distributions; income deciles; an example on inequality, taxes and subsidies; robust versus non-robust measures of spread; matching distributions to box plots.
Application of variance in descriptive analysis: measuring stunting; the WHO length/height-for-age standard, how it is built and summarised, and following one boy’s development against it.
The (standard) normal distribution: the z-score, why it is needed, standardisation, and exam examples on determining stunting status.
When univariate analysis is not enough: the Datasaurus, a synthetic dataset whose univariate summaries hide everything.
Reading before Week 4, homework examples on z-scores, variance and the normal distribution, a pointer to Our World in Data on income inequality, and the key concepts checklist.

title: Week 6 · Simple and multiple regression. Bias. Linearity
text:
What the deck covers

Example of an exam assignment (the t-test recap): a definition question, problem introduction, descriptive analysis, checks and balances, the effect of technology and of variety on rice yields, how to measure the effect of nitrogen fertiliser, and a framework for interpreting any statistical test.

Bias and efficiency: sampling from the population; unbiased and efficient, unbiased but inefficient, biased but efficient, biased and inefficient estimates.
Assumptions of the MLR: the six assumptions and what each group of them guarantees (unbiased; BLUE; classical linear model).
Assumption 1, linearity: can we draw a straight line through the dots; detection with residual plots; resolutions; common linear transformations; the Anscombe quartet.

Week 1 Prerequisites
Key prerequisite for this week is the undergraduate level of knowledge in statistics. This includes, but not limited to understanding the following concepts:

Mean, Median, Mode, Maximum, Minimum, Quantiles, Quartiles, Percentiles;
Box plot and Histogram;
Distribution, skew and kurtosis;
Power (\(x^a=b\)) and the logarithm transformation \(\log_a b = x\). Properties of the logarithm: \(\log_a 1=0\) and \(\log_a 0 = -\infty\) .

To bridge any of the knowledge gaps, you may follow materials prerecorded for you and available on Ilias:

Introduction to statistics and scale levels. Slides and Exercises
Basic measures. Slides
Understanding and visualizing data I. Slides and Exercises
Understanding and visualizing data II. Slides and Exercises


Optional materials
If materials mentioned above are insufficient, consider following the unit Summarizing quantitative data and Displaying and comparing quantitative data from the Khan academy. Specifically, you are encourage to pay close attention to:

Measuring center in quantitative data
Interquartile range (IQR)
Box and whisker plots
Displaying quantitative data with graphs with specific focus on the videos:

“Creating a histogram”, “Histograms” and “Interpreting a histogram”.

Introduction to Logarithm

Good controls in the RCT
The control group is a perfect counterfactual when three conditions are met:

has the same characteristics, on average, as the treatment group;
remains unaffected by the treatment; and
reacts to the treatment in the same way as the treatment group;



When these three conditions are met, the treatment causes the effect ceteris paribus (Gertler et al. 2016).




the average characteristics of the treatment group and the comparison group must be identical in the absence of the program.2 Although individual units in the treatment group don’t need to have “perfect clones” in the comparison group, on average the characteristics of treatment and comparison groups should be the same.
treatment should not affect the comparison group either directly or indirectly.
the outcomes of units in the control group should change the same way as outcomes in the treatment group if both groups were given the program (or not).

Is a statistical test use to conclude about the population based on a sample.

The Central Limit Theorem (2)
The estimate of the mean \(\hat{\mu}\) in the sample of the size \(n\)

tends to follow a normal distribution centered at the population’s mean \(\mu\),
with the standard error, \(\text{SE}(\hat{\mu})\) calculated based on the population’s standard deviation, \(\text{SE}(\hat{\mu}) = \sigma / \sqrt{n}\),
when two conditions are satisfied:

Independence. The sample is random.
Only for sample size below 30 obs (\(n < 30\)) Normality. The population is normally distributed.

The Central Limit Theorem (3)
In other words:

When our random sample is large enough

(or the population is normally distributed for small samples),

sample estimate of mean \(\hat{\mu}\) approximates the population mean \(\mu\):

\(\hat{\mu} \approx \mu\);

with the standard error that depends on the \(\sigma\) (pop. SD) and the sample size (\(n\)):

\(\text{SE}(\hat{\mu}) = \sigma / \sqrt{n}\).

Measures deviation (error) of the \(\hat{\mu}\) estimate, from the population parameter (\(\mu\)), accounting for the size of the sample (\(n\)).

\(H_0\) Null Hypothesis
The population mean equals to zero \(\mu_{0}\)

\(H_1\) Alternative Hypothesis
The population mean is not zero \(\mu_{0}\)

\(H_1: \mu > \mu_{0}\)

Sample SD: \(s = 3.3\)

Compute the t-statistics for the mean difference from zero.

\(\mu_0 = 0\)?
\(t = \frac{\sqrt{25} ( -2.2 - 0)}{3.3} \\ = 5 \cdot (-1/3) \\= -1.667\)




Compute the t-statistics for the mean difference from -5.5.

\(\mu_0 = -5.5\)?

text:
Step 3. Setting a decision rule (1)
To reject \(H_0\)

we compare t-statistics to a critical value \(c_{df, \text{CL}}\), with
\(\text{CL}\) - the confidence level

opposite to the significance level: \(\text{CL} = 1-\alpha\)

\(df\) - degrees of freedom

is the minimum values of the t-statistics when we can reject \(H_0\)

at the given confidence level, and
with the given degrees of freedom.

title: Week 05. Hypothesis testing II. Central Limit Theorem. T-distribution. Confidence intervals. t-test
text:
Step 3. Confidence level
Confidence level depends on the significance level (\(\alpha\)) and the alternative hypothesis:


when \(H_1: \mu \ne \mu_{0}\) we use a two-sided t-test, thus

\(\text{CL} = 1 - \alpha / 2\)





when \(H_1: \mu < \mu_{0}\) or \(H_1: \mu > \mu_{0}\) we use a one-sided t-test,

\(\text{CL} = 1 - \alpha\)




level of significance \(\alpha\);
-   $\alpha = 0.05$

title: Week 05. Hypothesis testing II. Central Limit Theorem. T-distribution. Confidence intervals. t-test
text:
Step 3. Degrees of freedom
the number of degrees of freedom \(df = n - k\):

\(n\) is the number of observation in the sample and
\(k\) is the number of parameters

\(k=1\) for the one-sample t-test \(k=2\) for the two-sample t-test

title: Week 05. Hypothesis testing II. Central Limit Theorem. T-distribution. Confidence intervals. t-test
text:
Step 3. Reject/Accept
We can reject \(H_0: \mu = \mu_0\) in favor of \(H_1: \mu \neq \mu_{0}\) only if:

the absolute value of the t-statistics is strictly greater then the critical value.


\(|t| > c_{df, 1 - \alpha / 2}\) for two-sided t-test \(H_1: \mu \ne \mu_{0}\)
\(|t| > c_{df, 1 - \alpha}\) for one-sided t-test \(H_1: \mu > \mu_{0}\) or \(H_1: \mu > \mu_{0}\)


In all other cases, we need to accept \(H_0\).

Population regression (PRF)


Always unknown

\[y = {\beta}_{0} + {\beta}_{1}x + u\]

What we learn from the sample of size \(n\), where \(i \in {1, 2, \dots, n}\)

\(\hat{\beta}_{1}\) - estimated slope

Regression: Coefficients
Regression parameters / coefficient (\(\hat{\beta}_0\) and \(\hat{\beta}_1\)) are estimated using the Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) method. These are:

The intercept: (\(\hat{\beta}_0\))

is the value of \(\hat{y}\), when all regressors (\(x\)) are zero.



The slope: (\(\hat{\beta}_1\))

change in the expected value of \(\hat{y}\) (in units of \(y\)), when \(x\) increases by one unit.

text:
Regression: OLS Algorithm
















































1 Proposes \(\hat{\beta_0}\) and \(\hat{\beta_1}\) so that actual values are: \(y_i = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 \cdot x_i + \hat{u}_i\)


2 Computes fitted values (\(\hat{y}_i = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 \cdot x_i\)) and residuals (\(\hat{u}_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i\)).


3 Computes squared residuals and the sum of it \(\sum \hat{u}^2\)


4 Repeats 1-3 with new estimates of \(\hat{\beta_0}\) and \(\hat{\beta_1}\);


5 Compare new sum of squared residuals \(\sum \hat{u}\) to the previous one.


6 Repeats 4-5 to minimize sum of squared residuals until it no longer reduces.


7 Estimates of \(\hat{\beta_0} = 656.15\) and \(\hat{\beta_1} = 810.95\) are values, where sum of squared residuals are minimal (\(\sum \hat{u}^2 = 530,480,825,704.7\)).

text:
George Udny Yule
In an 1899 MLR was used to link the administration of the English Poor Laws in different counties to the likelihood county residents were poor, while controlling for population growth and the age distribution in the county.

The poor laws provided subsistence for the indigent, usually by offering shelter and employment in institutions called workhouses.
Yule was particularly interested in whether the practice of outdoor relief, which provided income support for poor people without requiring them to move to a workhouse, increased poverty rates by making pauperism less onerous.
This is a well-defined causal question much like those that occupy social scientists today.
